messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Aroha, an eighty‑year‑old Māori welder who has spent her life turning metal into tools for her community, has carried the invisible weight of a decades‑old assault by the man she married. Their marriage began with promise, but on a July afternoon in the 1990s, the man—who had once been a promising carpenter—hit her in the shoulder while she was bent over a welding table, the metal sparks still flying from her torch. The blow left a bruise that never faded, a permanent reminder of the moment her body was no longer safe in his presence. Even after that day, he would return to the kitchen and press his fist into her arm in frustration, each strike leaving a fresh scar and a new sense of dread. In the weeks that followed, Aroha’s nights became a battleground. The thought that her body might fail again made her sleep fragile; she could not fall or stay asleep. When the darkness settled, she would wake with the instinct to check the doors, the windows, the familiar rustling of the shop’s ventilation system that now felt like an enemy. She would stand for long stretches, eyes wide, listening to the hiss of coolant and the hiss of her own breathing, convinced that if she didn’t stay alert, the next blow could come at any moment. The belief that her body was permanently damaged—an image that had crystallized from that first hit—fed into this threat, so that the more she felt her body’s unreliability, the more she stayed on guard. Her fear of injury was not just a residual echo; it was a living, breathing force that pulled her from sleep and into a constant state of readiness. That sleepless vigilance, in turn, hardened the very conviction that her body was beyond repair. Each night she stayed up, each moment of trembling awareness, reinforced the notion that she could never trust her own flesh again. The feeling of danger did not dissipate; instead, it seeped into her sense of self, convincing her that her capacity for normal emotion had been lost forever. The cycle of threat and appraisal grew tighter, each loop making her feel more isolated in her own home, despite the presence of her spouse, who now seemed to be a distant echo of the person who had once held her hand. The relentless cycle spilled over into her work. Aroha still walked into the welding shop on the edge of town every Thursday, where the bright glare of arc light and the clatter of metal would set her nerves alight. The hiss of the oxygen tank, the metallic scent of hot steel—these sensory cues triggered the same hypervigilance that kept her awake at night. She would pause before she could lift the torch, breathing heavily, the memory of the earlier blows flaring into her mind. Her fear of the shop’s environment forced her to skip shifts, to hand over tasks to younger apprentices, and eventually, to retire from the shop entirely. This avoidance of the very place that had once been her livelihood further isolated her, amplifying her belief that she was no longer capable of functioning safely. Now, at eighty, Aroha finds herself in a quiet room at the community health center, her heart racing as she speaks. She tells the therapist that she has lost the simple joys of her life: the quiet comfort of sleep, the sense of trust in her own body, and the ability to feel normal emotions. She is terrified that the cycle of threat and negative appraisal will never break. Yet, she also holds a fragile hope—that with time and help, she might learn to let go of the constant guard, to trust the metal beneath her hands and the silence of her own bedroom. Her present fear is not just of physical harm; it is the dread that she will never again feel safe enough to let herself rest, to let herself be vulnerable, and to let herself love again.
